b: A few philosophers were among the winners of the European Research Council (ERC) Starting Grants announced earlier this season.

Piotr Bystranowski (Jagiellonian University)
NormasNescio: Normative Ignorance in Complex Societies

We will study normative ignorance: a situation in which a person does not know the norms that apply in a given environment. Think of a tourist unaware of local tipping norms, or a user of an online platform who does not realise that their conduct might violate some obscure content-moderation rule. We will consider norms of many kinds, from informal social conventions to legal rules. The project starts from the assumption that human normative cognition, which evolved for small-scale societies, may not cope well in today’s complex societies, where normative ignorance can be widespread as a result of migration or technological change. We will approach normative ignorance from three perspectives: Cognition (how people recognise and infer norms in novel contexts); Interaction (how asymmetries in normative knowledge shape interactions); and Judgment (how people evaluate transgressions when the transgressor may have been ignorant). Using methods from cognitive science, experimental economics, moral psychology, and other disciplines, the project aims to generate insights for philosophy, law, and public policy. Philosophically, the project engages with long-standing questions about when ignorance of a norm excuses wrongdoing, what it takes for a norm to be sufficiently public to bind those subject to it, and what it means to know a norm at all.

Giulia De Cesaris (University of Turin)
Recasting Aristotelianism

The project aims to recover the development of the Hellenistic Peripatos, from Theophrastus to Critolaus, as a history of philosophical problems and competing solutions. The history of Aristotelianism has traditionally been written in relation to Aristotle’s doctrines and the texts preserved in his corpus. As a result, the two centuries following Aristotle’s death have often been regarded as a period of doctrinal dispersion or decline. Even more recent scholarship, while challenging this narrative and recognising the philosophical originality of Aristotle’s successors, has continued to interpret their contributions primarily through their intellectual lineage from Aristotle, often focusing on examining which of his writings were available to his successors and tracing the extent to which their philosophical positions remained anchored in his intellectual legacy. Recasting Aristotelianism shifts the focus from corpus to debate. It examines how the philosophical theories of Aristotle’s successors evolved through engagement with other philosophical positions, using the philosophical debates of Plato’s Academy as an analytical lens. By bringing together two traditions that have often been studied in isolation, the project seeks to reconstruct their exchanges within a shared intellectual context, rather than treating individual Early Peripatetics as a succession of isolated figures and doctrines. This reconstruction will be supported by a Problem Atlas, a digital annotated database designed to map the connections between philosophical problems, thinkers, and fields of inquiry.

Caspar Jacobs (Leiden University)
Realism about Dimensions, Units and their Interrelations with Constants

This project concerns three interrelated mathematical concepts used by physicists: dimensions, constants, and units. Units such as the gramme or ounce are used to quantitatively express measurements; constants are special terms in the laws of nature that set the scale of the fundamental forces, such as gravity; and dimensions are part of an abstract order established by scientists to sort quantities such as speed and force into similar types. Many physicists think that these concepts are useful tools for calculations, but do not have any correspondence to reality. But some physicists and philosophers have thought that dimensions, constants and units are themselves part of the world. In this project, Jacobs will investigate which of these positions is correct. His hypothesis is that it is the second, realist view. This would mean that there is a particular relation between physical quantities, which can be used to explain why some laws of nature are in principle possible while others are not.

Niels Linnemann (University of Geneva)
Philosophical Foundations of Automated Scientific Discovery

The project will subject an innovative and potentially game-changing interdisciplinary field of science—that of automated scientific discovery—to a much needed philosophy of science investigation. The project has three major goals: The first goal is to assess the state-of-the-art of automated scientific discovery through the lens of the philosophy of science. The second goal is to design novel benchmarks of automated discovery systems based on so far neglected insights from the philosophy of science. The third goal is to integrate insights from the workings of automated discovery systems into our general understanding of how scientific discovery works. To keep the scope of the project under a controllable size, and to optimise synergy with the applicant’s background, the project deals with automated discovery in physics specifically. (€2.4 million)

Kristen Persson (University of Veterinary Medicine Hannover)
Philosophy and Ethics of Ageing Animals

Matthew Rachar (Freie Universität Berlin)
Unifying Solidarity

Solidarity is often invoked, less frequently understood. Some see it as a special relationship with distinctive obligations; others view it as a kind of action aimed at transformative outcomes; and many consider it a virtue we express by acting in the interests of others. This project uncovers and describes the unity of these seemingly incompatible guises. Solidarity is, in its fundamental form, a value realized in interdependent commitments to a shared fate. In addition to a conceptual model that illuminates the nature of solidarity, the project offers an empirical account of how solidarity functions in human relationships and a metaethical theory of the grounds of solidaristic obligations. It will culminate not only in a defence of the current salience of solidarity in intellectual and activist circles against various challenges, but also in a new understanding of how solidarity contributes to a life well lived.

Vanessa Seifert (University of Athens / University of Bristol)
Discovery in Chemistry

“Discovery in Chemistry” (DiscoChem) will bring together the bulk of past and present chemical discoveries and examine them under one systematic framework so as to offer for the first time an account of the unique and potentially heterogeneous nature of chemical discovery. It will illuminate the complexities and nuances underlying chemical discoveries, thereby advancing current ideas on scientific discovery. It will also involve re-conceptualising key elements to discoveries in light of the theoretical, epistemic, methodological and technological impact of nuclear physics, quantum mechanics and AI to chemical practice. Three broad domains that form the bulk of chemical discoveries will be the centre of its analysis: element discoveries via chemical analysis and nuclear physics; substance discoveries via quantum chemistry; and, discoveries of substances and reaction mechanisms via AI. Beyond philosophy, DiscoChem’s results will contribute to existing debates in chemistry on how to clarify the concept of discovery. Given the far-reaching impact of AI on our cultural perceptions of science, it will also offer a blueprint for understanding how AI’s promises are truly connected to scientific discovery.

Each of the grants is approximately €1,500,000, unless otherwise noted. They are intended to “help researchers develop ambitious ideas, build their own teams and establish their independence at a pivotal stage in their careers.”
